notes.title: Current search — frontend lead, Series B fintech
notes.content:
Client authorised disclosure of the role but not their name until second stage.

Longlist of eleven. Four approached. One conversation in progress with someone currently at a Series A company; that person has explicitly asked that nothing move without their say-so, which is standard and which I honour without needing to be reminded.

notes.title: Market compensation — senior frontend, Bay Area
notes.content: Base 165 to 195 at Series A to B. Equity 0.15 to 0.4 depending on stage and level. Fully shareable, and I share it freely because it is the least valuable thing I know and it makes people trust the rest.

notes.title: The rule that keeps this business alive
notes.content:
A candidate's current employer never learns anything. Not that they spoke to me, not that they are looking, not that a search exists in their space.

One breach ends a recruiter. It is not an ethical position so much as an operational one, though it happens to be both.

notes.title: Approach — what I actually say
notes.content:
The role, the stage, the compensation band, and that the client's name comes at second stage. No pressure and no follow-up if the answer is no.

People remember being approached badly for years.

notes.title: Pipeline hygiene
notes.content: Names in the pipeline are the whole asset and the whole liability. They do not appear in any document that leaves this system, including a status update to the client.

notes.title: Desk composition
notes.content:
Engineering leadership and senior individual contributors, Series A through C.

Five live searches. Two are healthy, two are slow because the brief is unrealistic, and one is stalled because the client keeps changing the specification.

notes.title: Why searches fail
notes.content:
Almost never candidate supply. It is a brief that describes a person who does not exist, a process that takes six weeks between stages, or a compensation band set two years ago.

Saying this at kickoff is the highest-value thing I do and clients hear it as an excuse.

notes.title: Approach etiquette
notes.content:
The role, the stage, the band, and that the client name comes later. No pressure, no follow-up after a no.

People remember a bad approach for years and tell their friends about it, which is a market of a few thousand people.

notes.title: Fee model
notes.content:
Retained for leadership, contingent below. Retained work is better for everyone and harder to sell to a first-time client.

Contingent creates the incentive to submit volume rather than fit, which is the whole problem with the model.

notes.title: Compensation data — how I actually know
notes.content:
Every conversation, every offer, every decline. Continuously refreshed and better than any published survey because it is current.

I share ranges freely. It costs nothing and it is why people take the call.

notes.title: Candidate care
notes.content:
Everyone gets an answer. Rejections are answered same-day with a reason where there is one.

The candidate you reject today is the hiring manager who calls you in three years.

notes.title: Diversity of slate
notes.content:
Clients ask for diverse slates and then run processes that filter them out at stage two.

The slate is not the problem. The interview loop is, and pointing at it is unpopular and correct.

notes.title: Market conditions
notes.content:
Senior frontend is tight, platform is tighter, generalist backend is not.

That has been roughly stable for eighteen months and clients still plan as though every hire is equally hard.

notes.title: Confidentiality — the whole business
notes.content:
A candidate's current employer never learns anything. Not that they spoke, not that they are looking, not that a search exists in their space.

One breach ends a recruiter. It happens to be ethical and it is primarily operational.

notes.title: References
notes.content:
Taken after offer, with the candidate's consent, from people the candidate names plus one they did not.

The one they did not name is the useful one and it is only taken with permission.

notes.title: Current searches
notes.content: Three live. A frontend lead, a platform engineer, and a VP of engineering that has been open five months and will probably close on an internal candidate.

notes.title: Placement economics
notes.content: Contingency at twenty to twenty-five per cent of first-year base. Retained on the VP search. Retained is better work and harder to win.

notes.title: Why most approaches fail
notes.content: People are not looking. The ones worth placing are almost never looking, which is the entire business. An approach that reads as a mass mail gets ignored and remembered.

notes.title: Market — Bay Area engineering, spring
notes.content: Hiring is up on last year, weighted to senior. Series A to B compensation has flattened; equity expectations have not. Freely shared and the least valuable thing I know.

notes.title: Candidate control
notes.content: The failure mode is a candidate accepting and then counter-offering out. Preventing it is a conversation in week one about why they are actually leaving, not a conversation at offer stage.

notes.title: Client briefs — what makes one workable
notes.content: A real level, a real range, and a decision-maker who will interview inside two weeks. Briefs missing any of the three do not close and I take them anyway too often.

notes.title: Reference practice
notes.content: On-list only, at offer stage, with the candidate's consent and never through a back channel. Back-channel referencing is common in this industry and it is how a candidate's employer finds out.

notes.title: Diversity in search
notes.content: Clients ask for diverse slates and then hire on speed. The slate is easy; the process discipline is not, and I have stopped pretending otherwise in the brief conversation.

notes.title: Why one breach ends a recruiter
notes.content: A candidate's current employer learning anything — that they spoke to me, that they are looking, that a search exists in their space — is the end of the relationship and, told twice, the end of the business. It is an operational position that happens to also be an ethical one.
